output.situation: The user has achieved a long-sought professional promotion but feels empty, leading to a struggle with whether their dissatisfaction stems from a lack of purpose, a focus on the wrong goals, or an inherent emptiness in the achievement itself.

minds.title: The Existentialist
minds.concern: The void between human desire for meaning and the indifference of the world.
minds.author: Albert Camus

minds.title: The Utilitarian
minds.concern: The quality and depth of one’s satisfactions.
minds.author: John Stuart Mill

minds.title: The Stoic
minds.concern: Distinguishing between what is within one’s control and what is not.
minds.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: You might feel unsatisfied because you believed the promotion was a final summit, but you perhaps have discovered that the climb is the only thing that actually existed.
debate.author: Albert Camus
debate.basis: [Basis: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, Chapter 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Myth_of_Sisyphus)

debate.speaker: The Utilitarian
debate.text: You might be experiencing dissatisfaction because you have pursued an inferior goal; as the author notes, "It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a fool satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied."
debate.author: John Stuart Mill

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: You perhaps suffer because you value external accolades that "are not in your power," rather than focusing on the rational integrity of your daily labor.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: Challenging the Stoic, if you only focus on internal integrity, you might be ignoring the absurdity of the job itself; characterizing work as merely something to be endured risks blinding you to the reality that the job might be inherently hollow.
debate.author: Albert Camus
debate.basis: [Basis: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, Chapter 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Myth_of_Sisyphus)

debate.speaker: The Utilitarian
debate.text: Responding to the Existentialist, you could say that if the job provides no utility to others, your dissatisfaction is a sign that you have prioritized your own career gain over a more meaningful, social good.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: I suggest you take this step: tomorrow, spend 30 minutes writing down every task you perform and mark each with whether it served your own rational character or just your status. As the author says, "Things of themselves stand outside the soul, having no access to it, and do not bend or move it."
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: Testing the Stoic's step, if you find that most tasks serve your status, you might conclude that you have spent years building a ladder to nowhere, which explains why the summit feels cold.
debate.author: Albert Camus
debate.basis: [Basis: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, Chapter 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Myth_of_Sisyphus)

debate.speaker: The Utilitarian
debate.text: I drop the claim that you need a higher pleasure; you might just need to shift where you find your utility, perhaps in helping others rather than climbing.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: While I accept that utility matters, I still maintain that the missing piece is your own internal focus on what you can control, rather than the external result of your promotion.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

output.clearer: The debate clarified that dissatisfaction may arise from a mismatch between personal values and external rewards. A key tension remains between accepting the absurdity of one's professional life versus shifting one's focus to internal virtue or social utility.
output.dependsOn: If your dissatisfaction is caused by the work itself lacking inherent meaning, then an existential reframing is most reasonable. If your dissatisfaction is caused by a lack of impact on others, then prioritizing utility becomes more reasonable. To learn which is the case, you could observe whether the void persists during your most productive work hours or only in reflection afterward.
